entities.name: Louis of Toulouse
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Louis of Toulouse (1274–1297), born Louis of Anjou, was a pivotal figure in late 13th-century European dynastic and ecclesiastical politics, a Neapolitan prince who dramatically renounced his claim to the Kingdom of Naples for a life of mendicant piety. As the second son of King Charles II of Naples and Mary of Hungary, his unexpected choice to join the Franciscan Order and become a bishop challenged traditional notions of royal succession and spiritual vocation, leaving a lasting imprint on both the Capetian House of Anjou and the Franciscan movement. His brief life bridged the worlds of regal power and radical Christian poverty, making him a symbol of renunciation in an age of intense political and religious transformation.

Born in Brignoles, Provence, in 1274, Louis's early life was marked by political turmoil. From 1288 to 1295, he and his two brothers were held captive in Aragon as hostages following the War of the Sicilian Vespers (1282–1302), exchanged for their father, Charles II. During this seven-year captivity, Louis was educated by Franciscan friars, including Pietro di Giovanni Olivi, and developed a profound spiritual inclination. Upon his release and the death of his elder brother Charles Martel in 1295, Louis became heir apparent to the vast Angevin domains, including the Kingdom of Naples, Provence, and Anjou. However, in a dramatic and widely publicized act, he formally renounced his succession rights in favor of his younger brother, Robert, in December 1296, subsequently entering the Franciscan Order and being consecrated Bishop of Toulouse in February 1297 by Pope Boniface VIII.
